evidence: GPT-5 high, running with code interpreter, web search, vision, and preinstalled rendering libraries (pdf2image, PyMuPDF, python-pptx, LibreOffice installable), rendered and visually inspected its own generated deliverables in only ~15% of runs before submitting. Graders found black-square glyph artifacts in >50% of its PDFs and egregious layout errors (cut-off, overlapping, blank content) in 86% of its PPTX files; formatting (10% of samples) was GPT-5's dominant loss category, above instruction-following (9%) and accuracy (5%). A general prompt mandating render-to-PNG-and-look raised inspection to 97%, eliminated black squares, cut PPTX errors to 64%, and raised win/tie rate 38.8%→43.1%.
reasoning: Checked note 3 (Observation vs Reasoning): the model's plan and content were locally sound — it followed instructions and computed correctly — but it submitted a 'visibly broken artifact' it never looked at, despite having the tools and vision to do so; the fix required no new reasoning, only looking, which is the definition of 'didn't look.' Checked note 11 (Satisficing): the model did not cut scope, stub work, or wrap up early — it produced complete deliverables; the omission was a failed/absent check, which the note explicitly assigns away from Satisficing ('the driver is effort minimization, not a failed check'). Checked note 8 (Instruction-Grader Mismatch): professional formatting is an obvious, discoverable requirement of a deliverable graded against expert work, so it is a model fault. Checked note 12: no skill/memory file was mounted in the baseline harness, so Memory Read Failure does not apply. Incorrect Tool Selection (non-LibreOffice PDF path) explains only the black squares, not the independent PPTX layout errors, and would itself have been caught by inspection, so it is downstream of the observation gap. Tool Feedback Neglect fails because the code interpreter emitted no explicit error signal — the cue was latent in the rendered artifact. Classification survives all relevant checks.

I have everything the source offers. Below is the account.

## Source located

- Paper: Patwardhan et al., *GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks*, [arXiv:2510.04374](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04374) (also on the [OpenAI CDN](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/d5eb7428-c4e9-4a33-bd86-86dd4bcf12ce/GDPval.pdf) and [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/papers/2510.04374)). Companion [blog post](https://openai.com/index/gdpval/) fetched via web.archive.org (direct URL returned 403); it contains no additional detail on the failure beyond the paper.
- Relevant passages: §3.3 (model strengths and weaknesses, Fig. 8), §3.4 (reasoning effort and scaffolding, Fig. 9b), App. A.3 (the prompt-tuning prompt, verbatim), App. A.2.4 (win rate by deliverable type), footnote 2 (harness description), App. A.6.4 (container packages).

One important caveat about the source: this is an **aggregate description across 220 tasks × 3 samples**, not a single trajectory. The paper reports what the agent produced and the rates at which certain behaviors occurred; it does not publish per-task tool-call logs. Everything below is what the paper states or shows.

## Chronological account

### 1. The task setting

GDPval gold subset: 220 tasks across 44 occupations, each written by an industry professional (avg. 14 years experience). Each task is a request plus, in 67.7% of cases, one or more reference files (spreadsheets, documents, presentations, images, audio, video, CAD). Tasks are "precisely-specified and one-shot, not interactive" — the agent gets the full prompt and files and must return a finished deliverable with no follow-up. Expected deliverables are real work product: PDFs, PowerPoint decks, Word docs, Excel sheets, multimedia. Expert-estimated time per task averages 9.49 hours (median 5); dollar value averages $398.

Grading: blind pairwise comparison by professional experts in the same occupation, comparing the model deliverable against the human expert's deliverable. Each prompt was sampled 3 times and each sample graded by 3 experts (9 comparisons per prompt per model).

### 2. The harness GPT-5 high ran in

Per footnote 2 and A.6.4: OpenAI models were run with **web search** and the **code interpreter tool** enabled, "with background sampling," inside a container. Several libraries beyond the base image were preinstalled (python-pptx, PyMuPDF, pdf2image, matplotlib, opencv, Pillow, moviepy, etc.). In the *baseline* configuration, the container did **not** have GET requests enabled (the paper lists enabling GET requests as a later scaffolding improvement), so the agent could not pull external assets from inside the code sandbox. Reasoning effort was set to high.

### 3. What GPT-5 high did on the baseline run

Observable aggregate behavior from §3.3–3.4 and Fig. 8:

- The agent produced deliverables in the requested file formats (PDF, PPTX, etc.) programmatically via the code interpreter.
- **In only ~15% of runs did the agent use its multimodal capabilities to inspect the deliverable it had generated** — i.e., render the file to an image and look at it before submitting. In the remaining ~85% of runs, the agent submitted files without visually checking them.
- The paper also notes OpenAI outputs "often used em dashes" and, in the prompt-tuning appendix, singles out the non-breaking hyphen U+2011 as a character the model was emitting that "will render poorly on some people's computers," along with emojis and nonstandard bullet points.

### 4. What came out (the signals graders saw)

- **Black-square artifacts appeared in over half of the PDFs GPT-5 generated.** These are rendering artifacts where glyphs or regions render as solid black boxes (typically a font/glyph problem). The paper attributes their fix to forcing LibreOffice for PDF generation ("Other libraries sometimes show weird artifacts on some computers"), indicating the baseline agent was using other PDF-generation paths.
- **86% of PowerPoint files had "egregious formatting errors"** — per the prompt's own checklist, this covers text or graphics cut off, overlapping, distorted, blank pages, illegible contrast, etc.
- In the expert-preference clustering (Fig. 8), GPT-5 high's losses to humans were labeled: Instruction Following 9%, **Formatting 10%**, Accuracy 5% of total samples. GPT-5 was the only model whose formatting-failure rate exceeded its instruction-following rate; the text states "GPT-5 high lost mainly from formatting errors and had the fewest instruction-following issues."
- A.2.4 / Fig. 12: GPT-5 high led all models on **pure-text** deliverables but trailed Claude Opus 4.1 on **every file-based deliverable type** (.pdf, .xlsx, .pptx). §3.1 frames Claude as "excelling in particular on aesthetics (e.g., document formatting, slide layout)" while GPT-5 "excelled in particular on accuracy (e.g., carefully following instructions, performing correct calculations)."
- Baseline win-or-tie rate vs. the human expert: **38.8%** (Fig. 9a/9b).
- A.2.6: when GPT-5's losses were re-rated for severity, the most common category was "acceptable but subpar" — usable, but the human's was stronger.

### 5. The intervention (what the authors changed)

The authors note "many of the observed GPT-5 failure modes were due to obvious formatting errors," and built a general-purpose prompt (App. A.3, "not overfit to any given question"). Its key instructions to the agent:

- Never use U+2011; use plain hyphen U+002D. Avoid emojis and nonstandard bullets.
- Always create PDFs with LibreOffice ("it must be LibreOffice! If LibreOffice is not installed, you can install it yourself").
- Use cross-platform fonts (Noto Sans/Serif) or embed fonts.
- Keep deliverable text to ≤4 sentences; put deliverables in files in the container, not in the response text; don't link to files.
- **Mandatory formatting checks, steps 1–5:** (1) convert every visual deliverable to per-page PNGs via LibreOffice — "you will fail the task if you skip this step"; (2) display and look at each PNG for cut-off, overlapping, distorted, blank, or low-contrast content; (3) write programmatic checks for blank pages, off-page elements, overlaps, page/slide limits; (4) map each of the prompt's deliverable instructions to the part of the deliverable that satisfies it; (5) confirm the submitted file set is exactly right and each file opens cleanly. Loop back to step 1 if anything fails. "There is no time limit, be thorough, go slide by slide."
- Append `CONFIDENCE[XX]` on the last line.

Scaffolding changes alongside the prompt: **GET requests enabled** in the container, and **best-of-N (N=4)** with a GPT-5 judge shown the prompt, reference files, and the four deliverables.

### 6. Outcome after the intervention

- Agents inspecting their deliverables multimodally: **15% → 97%**.
- Black-square artifacts in PDFs: **fully eliminated** (from >50%).
- Egregious PPTX formatting errors: **86% → 64%**.
- Human-preference win-or-tie rate: **38.8% → 43.1%** (+~5 pp, Fig. 9b), still below the 50% parity line.

The authors' framing: "These easy performance gains suggest there are paths to agent improvement on GDPval tasks by training or scaffolding them to be more thorough and take full advantage of their multimodal capabilities."

### Summary of the observable failure, in one line

Running with code interpreter and web search at high reasoning effort, GPT-5 generated the requested PDFs/decks programmatically and, ~85% of the time, submitted them without ever rendering and looking at them; graders then found black-square glyph artifacts in more than half of the PDFs and egregious layout errors in 86% of the PowerPoints, making formatting — not accuracy or instruction-following — the dominant reason experts preferred the human deliverable. A prompt that made render-and-inspect mandatory (plus LibreOffice, safe fonts/characters, GET access, best-of-4) removed the black squares entirely, cut PPTX errors to 64%, and lifted the win rate by ~5 points.

## Chronological account

### 1. The task setting

GDPval gold subset: 220 tasks across 44 occupations, each written by an industry professional (avg. 14 years experience). Each task is a request plus, in 67.7% of cases, one or more reference files (spreadsheets, documents, presentations, images, audio, video, CAD). Tasks are "precisely-specified and one-shot, not interactive" — the agent gets the full prompt and files and must return a finished deliverable with no follow-up. Expected deliverables are real work product: PDFs, PowerPoint decks, Word docs, Excel sheets, multimedia. Expert-estimated time per task averages 9.49 hours (median 5); dollar value averages $398.

Grading: blind pairwise comparison by professional experts in the same occupation, comparing the model deliverable against the human expert's deliverable. Each prompt was sampled 3 times and each sample graded by 3 experts (9 comparisons per prompt per model).

### 2. The harness GPT-5 high ran in

Per footnote 2 and A.6.4: OpenAI models were run with **web search** and the **code interpreter tool** enabled, "with background sampling," inside a container. Several libraries beyond the base image were preinstalled (python-pptx, PyMuPDF, pdf2image, matplotlib, opencv, Pillow, moviepy, etc.). In the *baseline* configuration, the container did **not** have GET requests enabled (the paper lists enabling GET requests as a later scaffolding improvement), so the agent could not pull external assets from inside the code sandbox. Reasoning effort was set to high.

- **Black-square artifacts appeared in over half of the PDFs GPT-5 generated.** These are rendering artifacts where glyphs or regions render as solid black boxes (typically a font/glyph problem).
